regional.syndrome: Sudden high fever with severe, often symmetrical polyarthralgia and rash; the name means 'that which bends up'. Arthritis persists for months to years in 30–40%. Neonatal infection from intrapartum transmission and neurological disease in older adults can be severe; deaths occur mainly via decompensation of comorbidity.
regional.headline: Alphavirus of the Semliki Forest complex causing explosive epidemics of febrile polyarthritis.
regional.prevention: Vector control; the virus-like particle vaccine Vimkunya is licensed from 12 years of age. The live-attenuated IXCHIQ was licensed first, but its US licence was suspended in August 2025 and the application withdrawn in January 2026 after vaccine-strain encephalitis and other serious adverse events.
regional.geography: Africa, Asia, Indian Ocean, Americas since 2013, with autochthonous outbreaks in southern Europe.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.incubation: Decades. Myelopathy appears after years; leukaemia typically forty to sixty years after perinatal infection.
regional.syndrome: Lifelong asymptomatic carriage in over 90%. Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL) appears after a latency of forty to sixty years, usually in those infected through breastfeeding, with a lifetime risk of a few per cent; HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) in under 4%, presenting as spastic paraparesis with bladder dysfunction. Also infective dermatitis of childhood, uveitis, and Strongyloides hyperinfection, the last because the virus distorts the Th2 response that normally contains the worm.
regional.headline: The first human retrovirus discovered, infecting 5-10 million people. Most carry it for life without consequence; a minority develop adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma after decades, or a progressive myelopathy.
regional.prevention: Avoiding breastfeeding by carrier mothers where safe alternatives exist, which is what cut transmission in Nagasaki; leucodepletion and donor screening of blood; condoms; not sharing injecting equipment. No vaccine.
regional.geography: Sharply defined endemic foci rather than a global distribution: south-western Japan, the Caribbean, parts of South America, West and Central Africa, Iran, Romania, and Aboriginal communities of central Australia, where some adult seroprevalences exceed 40%.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Bunyamwera and Germiston viruses: self-limiting fever with headache, rash and arthralgia. Ngari virus: documented haemorrhagic fever outbreaks in Kenya and Somalia, originally mistaken for Rift Valley fever.
regional.headline: Prototype orthobunyavirus. Its reassortant member Ngari virus (Bunyamwera backbone with Batai M segment) causes haemorrhagic fever in East Africa.
regional.geography: Sub-Saharan Africa; Xingu virus in South America.

regional.syndrome: Abrupt fever, profound weakness, myalgia, then vomiting and high-volume diarrhoea with electrolyte derangement, shock and sometimes haemorrhage. Survivors experience uveitis, arthralgia and neurological sequelae; virus persists in semen, aqueous humour and CSF, enabling late sexual transmission and relapse.
regional.headline: Filovirus causing Ebola disease, with case fatality historically 25–90%; now treatable with monoclonal antibodies and preventable by vaccination.
regional.prevention: The rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Ervebo) used in ring vaccination, plus the Ad26/MVA regimen; safe burial practices and infection prevention and control.
regional.geography: Central and West Africa — the 2013–2016 West African epidemic caused over 28,000 cases.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Dengue fever: high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia ('breakbone fever'), rash. A minority progress at defervescence to dengue with warning signs or severe dengue — plasma leakage, shock, haemorrhage and organ impairment. Secondary infection with a different serotype raises severe-disease risk through antibody-dependent enhancement.
regional.headline: The most important arboviral infection of humans worldwide, with an estimated 100–400 million infections annually.
regional.prevention: Vector control, Wolbachia-based mosquito replacement, and the live-attenuated vaccines CYD-TDV (serostatus-restricted) and TAK-003.
regional.geography: Tropics and subtropics worldwide; expanding with vector range.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.
